title: GitOps with Argo CD
intro: In Part 7 you ran hello-devops on Kubernetes by typing kubectl commands. Part 8 hands the deploying to Argo CD: git holds the desired state, and a controller in the cluster keeps the cluster equal to it. Day 39 sets up Argo CD and shows drift, self-heal and rollback. Day 40 adds dev and prod, promotion by pull request, and the habits teams use for image updates, secrets and access.

lessons.goal: By the end you can install Argo CD on your kind cluster, let it deploy hello-devops from your GitHub repo, and fix drift and roll back using only git.

sections.h: Why applying from a laptop stops working
sections.body:
All through Part 7 you deployed with `kubectl apply -k k8s` from your laptop. For one person and one cluster, that is fine. Add a few colleagues and it breaks in quiet ways:
- Someone fixes a Deployment by hand at night and never tells git.
- Two people apply from two branches, and the last one wins.
- Nobody can say which commit is running right now.
- Every laptop or pipeline that deploys holds a key that can change the cluster.

A difference between git and what really runs is called **drift**. You met it with Terraform on Day 27. A hand change made the real world differ from the code, and Terraform noticed only when you ran `plan` again.

**GitOps** closes that gap from the other side. Git becomes the only place where changes happen. A program inside the cluster keeps the cluster equal to git, all the time, whether or not anyone deploys. The [OpenGitOps project](https://opengitops.dev/), part of the CNCF, sums it up in four principles. The desired state must be:
- Declarative: you describe what you want, not the steps to get there.
- Versioned and immutable: it is stored with its full history, and old versions never change.
- Pulled automatically: software agents fetch it by themselves.
- Continuously reconciled: agents keep comparing the real system with it and fix differences.

Two of these should feel familiar. Kubernetes YAML is declarative, and on Day 30 you watched controllers reconcile: they compare what you asked for with what exists, then close the gap. GitOps runs the same kind of loop one level up, with git as the thing you asked for.

sections.body:
A new version can reach a cluster in two ways.

In a push deploy, something outside the cluster sends the change in. Your CI pipeline ends with `kubectl apply` or `helm upgrade`. So CI holds a key that can write to the cluster, and any workflow that can read that secret can change production. The deploy also happens only while the pipeline runs. If someone edits the cluster an hour later, nothing notices.

In a pull deploy, an agent runs inside the cluster. It reads git and applies what it finds. CI builds the image and changes a file in git, and that is all CI does. The pull model gives you:
- No cluster keys in CI, because the agent already lives in the cluster.
- A deploy log at no extra cost: `git log` shows who changed what, and when.
- Review before deploy, because every change can be a pull request.
- Rollback with `git revert`.
- Drift detection all day, even when nobody is deploying.

The price is one more system to install, upgrade and learn. On your laptop that means seven extra Pods. For any cluster that more than one person touches, I think the pull model is worth that price.

One thing does not change: CI still tests the code and builds the image, exactly as in Part 4. GitOps replaces only the last step, the one that touches the cluster.

sections.h: What Argo CD is made of
sections.body:
Argo CD is a GitOps agent for Kubernetes, part of the Argo project in the CNCF. It runs as a set of Pods in its own namespace, `argocd`. After the install you will see seven:
- `argocd-server`: the API server behind the web UI and the `argocd` command line tool.
- `argocd-repo-server`: clones your repo and turns a folder into plain YAML. It understands Kustomize and Helm (Argo CD 3.5 ships with Helm 4).
- `argocd-application-controller`: compares the cluster with that YAML and applies the difference. This is the reconcile loop.
- `argocd-applicationset-controller`: makes many Applications from one template (Day 40).
- `argocd-redis`: a cache for rendered YAML and app state.
- `argocd-dex-server`: connects Argo CD to single sign-on, such as GitHub or Google accounts.
- `argocd-notifications-controller`: sends messages, for example to Slack when a sync fails.

You tell Argo CD what to deploy with an Application. It is a custom resource: a new object type that a tool adds to Kubernetes. You write it as YAML and apply it like a Deployment. It has three main parts:
- A source: the repo URL, the branch (`targetRevision`) and the folder (`path`).
- A destination: which cluster and which namespace.
- A project: rules about what this app may touch. Everything starts in the project called `default`.

How does Argo CD remember which objects belong to which app? Since version 3.0 it writes an annotation on every object it applies, `argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id`. Older versions used a label for this, and many blog posts still say so. The worked example below shows the annotation on a real object.

sections.body:
The install is one long YAML file from the Argo CD project. The exact command is in the Commands list below, and two of its flags need explaining.

`kubectl apply --server-side` lets the API server work out the changes. You need it because one of Argo CD's custom resource definitions, the one for ApplicationSets, is too big for normal apply. Normal (client-side) apply stores a full copy of each object in an annotation, and annotations are limited to 262 KB in total. Server-side apply keeps no such copy. `--force-conflicts` lets the install take over fields that an earlier apply set, which matters when you upgrade.

Older videos are a common trap here. They show a plain `kubectl apply -n argocd -f install.yaml`, and on Argo CD 3.x that fails with an error about annotations that are too long.

The install URL points at the `stable` branch, which is fine on a laptop. At work you pin a version, with a tag such as `v3.5.6` in the URL instead of `stable`. Then an install today and an install next month give the same result.

Argo CD's web UI is not reachable from outside the cluster. On a laptop, `kubectl port-forward` is the simplest way in. Use local port 8443, because 8080 may still be busy from your Terraform work in Part 6. The browser warns about the certificate, because the install makes a self-signed one. That is expected here.

Log in as `admin` with the password from `argocd admin initial-password -n argocd`. Out of the box, `admin` is the only user, and it may do everything. Teams connect single sign-on and give people narrower roles; Day 40 shows the pieces. Install the `argocd` CLI with Homebrew and log it in through the same port-forward.

sections.body:
Every Application shows two separate statuses. Beginners often read them as one.

Sync status answers one question: does the cluster match git?
- `Synced`: every object Argo CD manages matches the YAML in git.
- `OutOfSync`: at least one object differs, is missing, or should be gone.

Health answers a different question: does it work?
- `Healthy`: for a Deployment, all replicas are updated and available.
- `Progressing`: not healthy yet but still moving, such as a rollout in progress.
- `Degraded`: failed, for example a rollout that ran past its deadline.
- `Missing`: in git, but not in the cluster yet.
- `Suspended` and `Unknown` show up less often.

The two are independent. Push a typo in an image tag, and the app is Synced (the cluster has exactly what git says) but not Healthy (the new Pods cannot pull the image). Make a hand edit to a label, and the app is OutOfSync but still Healthy. The health of a whole app is the worst health of its parts.

How fast does Argo CD see a new commit? By default it checks git about every three minutes: 120 seconds plus a random delay of up to 60 seconds, so that many apps do not all ask at once. Press Refresh in the UI, or run `argocd app get hello-devops --refresh`, to check now. Teams whose Argo CD has a public address add a git webhook, so a push triggers a check at once. GitHub cannot reach your kind cluster, so here you poll.

Changes inside the cluster are different. The controller watches the objects it manages, so it sees a `kubectl edit` within seconds.

sections.body:
Out of the box, Argo CD only reports differences. You press Sync, in the UI or with `argocd app sync`, and it applies git. Automated sync applies new commits by itself. Two more switches decide how strict it is:
- `selfHeal: true` undoes changes made in the cluster but not in git, such as a `kubectl edit`.
- `prune: true` deletes objects you removed from git. Without it, they stay, and Argo CD only marks them for pruning.

Both are off by default, a careful choice for a tool that can delete things. With automated sync alone, a hand edit makes the app OutOfSync and stays in place until the next commit. The lab's `argocd/application.yaml` turns both on.

This part trips most people up: Argo CD is not the only controller that changes your objects. On Day 35 you added a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA), which raises the replica count under load. Argo CD sees 5 replicas where git says 3 and, with self-heal on, sets it back. The HPA raises it again. They fight for as long as the load lasts.

There are two ways out:
- Leave `replicas` out of the Deployment in git, so there is nothing to compare. The [Argo CD best practices](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/best_practices/) page suggests this.
- Tell Argo CD to ignore that one field. The lab does this with `ignoreDifferences` on `/spec/replicas`, plus the sync option `RespectIgnoreDifferences=true` so that a sync leaves the field alone too.

The lab takes the second way because `k8s/deployment.yaml` keeps `replicas: 3`. That keeps `kubectl apply -k k8s` working on its own, without Argo CD.

sections.body:
With GitOps, a rollback is a commit. You undo the bad change in git, and Argo CD deploys the state from before:
1. `git log --oneline -3` shows the recent commits.
2. `git revert <sha>` makes a new commit that undoes the bad one. History stays intact.
3. `git push`, then wait for the next check or run `argocd app sync hello-devops`.

Why not `kubectl rollout undo` from Day 32? It changes the cluster but not git, so with self-heal on, Argo CD puts the bad version straight back. Argo CD has its own `argocd app rollback` command, which redeploys an earlier entry from `argocd app history`. It refuses to run while automated sync is on, for the same reason: git must stay the source of truth.

In a real emergency, follow this order:
1. Turn off automated sync for that one app.
2. Fix the cluster by hand, and write down every change.
3. Put the same fix into git.
4. Turn automated sync back on.

Skip step 3, and the next sync quietly undoes your fix.

steps.say: See how Argo CD marks what it owns. Every object it applied carries a tracking annotation: the app name, then group and kind, then namespace and name. A ConfigMap belongs to the core group, which has an empty name, so nothing stands before the slash.

Now play the colleague who fixes things by hand. Change the greeting in the live ConfigMap and skip git. A `kubectl scale` would make a poor demo, because the lab tells Argo CD to ignore the replica count.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello patch configmap hello-config --type merge \
    -p '{"data":{"GREETING":"Edited by hand"}}'
configmap/hello-config patched

steps.say: The application controller watches every object it manages, so it sees the change at once. If you are quick, you catch the app OutOfSync. It stays Healthy, because the app still runs fine. Self-heal then syncs git's version back after a short pause.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n argocd get applications
NAME           SYNC STATUS   HEALTH STATUS
hello-devops   OutOfSync     Healthy

steps.say: Wait a few seconds and read the value again. Git's text is back, and you did nothing.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello get configmap hello-config -o jsonpath='{.data.GREETING}'
Hello from Kubernetes!

steps.say: To change the greeting for good, change git. Edit `k8s/configmap.yaml`, commit and push, then sync instead of waiting up to three minutes. Pods read environment variables only when they start (Day 34), so restart the Deployment to see the new text.
steps.code:
$ git commit -am "Change the greeting"
$ git push
$ argocd app sync hello-devops
$ kubectl -n hello rollout restart deployment hello-devops

code.title: argocd/application.yaml
code.src:
# An Argo CD Application: "keep the cluster equal to the k8s/ folder in git".
# Apply it once:  kubectl apply -n argocd -f argocd/application.yaml
# Replace <your-github-user> with your GitHub user name first.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  # Applications live in the namespace where Argo CD runs.
  namespace: argocd
  # When you delete this Application, also delete the things it created.
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
spec:
  project: default
  # Where the desired state lives: your repo, branch main, folder k8s.
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/<your-github-user>/hello-devops
    targetRevision: main
    path: k8s
  # Where to deploy: the same cluster Argo CD runs in, namespace hello.
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: hello
  # The autoscaler (k8s/hpa.yaml) changes the number of replicas while the app runs.
  # Ignore that one field, so Argo CD and the autoscaler do not fight.
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      name: hello-devops
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true # delete things that you removed from git
      selfHeal: true # undo changes made by hand in the cluster
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true # create namespace hello if it is missing
      - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true # also skip /spec/replicas when syncing

lessons.mistake: Fixing something in the cluster by hand and expecting the fix to stay. With self-heal on, Argo CD undoes `kubectl edit`, `kubectl scale` and even `kubectl delete` within seconds. With self-heal off, the fix lasts only until the next sync. Make the change in git and let Argo CD apply it. explain_back.prompt: Explain GitOps to a teammate in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention who applies changes, what self-heal does, and how you roll back.
explain_back.answer: With GitOps, git holds the desired state of the cluster, and an agent inside the cluster, Argo CD here, applies it. Nobody runs kubectl apply by hand: a change is a commit, usually through a pull request, and CI never needs a cluster key. Argo CD keeps comparing the cluster with git, and self-heal undoes changes that skipped git. To roll back, you revert the commit, and Argo CD deploys the old state.

check.q: The hello-devops app shows Synced and Degraded. What does that tell you?
options: The cluster matches git, but what git describes does not work
Someone edited the cluster by hand since the last sync
Argo CD cannot reach your GitHub repo right now
Prune is off, so old objects are still in the cluster
check.why: Synced means live equals git; Degraded means the objects fail, so the problem is in what you committed, such as a bad image tag.

check.q: You delete `redis.yaml` from git and push. Automated sync is on, but prune is off. What happens to Redis in the cluster?
options: It is deleted at the next sync
Argo CD puts redis.yaml back into your repo
It keeps running, and Argo CD marks it for pruning
The sync fails and nothing else deploys
check.why: Without prune, automated sync never deletes anything. The object stays, flagged as no longer in git, until someone prunes it.

check.q: A bad release is live, and self-heal is on. A colleague runs `kubectl rollout undo` (Day 32) to fix it fast. What happens next?
options: The rollback stays until the next commit
Argo CD writes the older version into git
The Deployment is deleted and created again
Argo CD puts the bad version back, because git still says so
check.why: Self-heal makes the cluster match git, and git still holds the bad version. Revert in git instead.

interview.q: What is GitOps, and how is it different from a CI pipeline that runs kubectl apply?
interview.a: GitOps keeps the desired state of a system in git, and an agent such as Argo CD or Flux pulls it and keeps the system equal to it. A push pipeline runs kubectl apply from outside, so it needs cluster credentials, and it only acts while it runs. The GitOps agent runs inside the cluster, keeps reconciling, and can undo drift. Every change is a commit, so review, history and rollback come from normal git tools.

interview.q: How do you roll back a bad deploy in an Argo CD setup?
interview.a: I revert the commit, or the pull request, that introduced the change and push, so git again describes the last good state. Argo CD syncs, and the cluster follows. Argo CD has its own rollback command, but it refuses to run while automated sync is on, and it would leave the cluster different from git. A git revert keeps one source of truth and leaves an audit trail.

interview.q: What do sync status and health status mean in Argo CD?
interview.a: Sync status compares the cluster with git: Synced means they match, OutOfSync means something differs. Health says whether the objects work, for example whether a Deployment's replicas are updated and available. They are independent. A bad image tag gives Synced but Degraded, and a harmless hand edit gives OutOfSync but Healthy. I check both before I call a deploy done.

deeper.body:
On Day 30 you saw that a controller has to know which objects are its own. A ReplicaSet uses labels and owner references. Argo CD has the same problem on a bigger scale: one cluster can hold objects from many Applications, plus objects that other controllers create.

Since 3.0, Argo CD tracks objects with the annotation `argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id`, in the form `app:group/Kind:namespace/name`. Before 3.0 the default was the label `app.kubernetes.io/instance`. That label caused two kinds of trouble:
- Other tools copy labels, for example an operator that copies its labels onto the objects it creates. A copied label could make Argo CD think it owned those objects.
- Label values may be at most 63 characters, so long app names were cut short.

The annotation names the exact object it sits on. If a tool copies it onto a different object, the name inside no longer matches, and Argo CD ignores the copy. You can still switch to label tracking in the `argocd-cm` ConfigMap, but there is rarely a reason to.

Argo CD also ignores some objects on purpose. Since 3.0 its default settings exclude kinds that change all the time, such as EndpointSlice, Endpoints and Lease. EndpointSlices change every time a Pod becomes ready or not ready (Day 33). Watching all of them would load the API server for no benefit, because nobody keeps them in git anyway.

Inside one object, Argo CD skips the `status` part by default, since the cluster writes it. You add your own exceptions with `ignoreDifferences`, as the lab does for replicas. Use it narrowly. Each ignored field is a place where git no longer tells the whole truth.

Finally, an object that lives in the app's namespace but in no Application is an orphaned resource. Argo CD never deletes it, because it never created it. A project can turn on warnings for orphaned resources with `orphanedResources`. That is a cheap way to spot leftovers from hand-made experiments, as long as the namespaces are small.

For hello-devops this all runs quietly in the background. It starts to matter when a second tool, such as a service mesh or an operator, writes to the same objects as Argo CD. Then `ignoreDifferences` and tracking decide who wins.

lessons.title: GitOps in practice: environments, promotion and image updates
lessons.goal: By the end you can run hello-devops as dev and prod from one ApplicationSet, promote a tested version from dev to prod with a pull request, and pick a safe way to keep secrets out of a GitOps repo.

guess.q: Version 1.2.0 runs well in dev. In a GitOps setup, how do you move it to prod?
options: Rebuild the image from the main branch for prod
Run `kubectl set image` in the prod namespace
Copy the 1.2.0 tag into the prod folder with a pull request
Click Sync on the prod app in the Argo CD UI
guess.why: Promotion is a change in git: prod gets the exact tag that dev already runs. A rebuild could ship different bytes, a kubectl edit gets undone, and Sync only applies what git already says.

terms.plain: A git repo that holds only deployment files, kept apart from the app's source code.
One running copy of the app with one purpose, such as dev for testing or prod for users.
A Kustomize folder that takes the shared base files and changes a few settings for one environment.

sections.body:
So far hello-devops keeps everything in one repo: the app code at the top, the Kubernetes YAML in `k8s/`. Teams usually pick one of three layouts:
- One repo per app, with code and YAML together. This is what you have now.
- An app repo for the code, plus a separate config repo that holds only YAML for every environment.
- A monorepo: one big repo for many apps, with a folder per app and per environment.

The [Argo CD best practices](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/best_practices/) page recommends a separate config repo. Its reasons, in short:
- You can change a replica count without starting a full CI build.
- The config history reads like a deploy log, without code commits in between.
- One config repo can deploy an app built from several code repos as one unit.
- Access can differ: many people may change code, while few may change prod.
- CI that commits YAML into the code repo can trigger itself in a loop.

That last point needs care in GitHub Actions. A push made with the workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not start new workflow runs, which stops most loops. A push made with a personal token does start them.

For one person and a laptop cluster, one repo is fine, and this lesson keeps it. The cost is small: a commit that changes only `overlays/` still runs `ci.yml` on main. If that bothers you, add `overlays/**` to the `paths-ignore` list of its push trigger.

sections.body:
An environment is one running copy of the app with one purpose. Dev is where new versions land first, and prod is what users see. Real teams usually give prod its own cluster. Here both live in your kind cluster, in the namespaces `hello-dev` and `hello-prod`.

On Day 37 you built two Kustomize overlays, `overlays/dev` and `overlays/prod`. Each one takes the shared files in `k8s/` and changes a few things. Dev runs one Pod and answers "Hello from dev!". Prod runs four, with more memory and a PodDisruptionBudget. Both turn the Service into a ClusterIP, so they do not fight the Day 39 app over NodePort 30080. `kubectl kustomize overlays/prod` prints exactly what prod gets.

Argo CD needs one Application per environment. You could copy `application.yaml` twice and change three lines in each copy. An **ApplicationSet** writes those copies for you. It has two parts:
- Generators produce a list of values. The lab uses the list generator with two entries, `env: dev` and `env: prod`.
- A template is an ordinary Application with placeholders such as `{{.env}}`. The controller fills it in once per entry.

Apply `argocd/applicationset.yaml`, and two Applications appear: `hello-devops-dev` and `hello-devops-prod`. Add a third entry, and a third app appears. Delete the ApplicationSet, and its Applications go too, along with everything they deployed. Other generators read their list from elsewhere: folders in a git repo, the clusters Argo CD knows, or open pull requests.

You will also meet app of apps: one parent Application whose folder holds only other Application files. It came first, and it still works. The Argo CD docs recommend ApplicationSets for most cases. They call app of apps an admin-only tool, because anyone who can push to that folder can create apps in any project.

sections.body:
**Promotion** means moving a version that passed in one environment on to the next. In GitOps it is a small change to text in git:
1. CI builds `ghcr.io/<you>/hello-devops:1.2.0` once, when you push the tag `v1.2.0` (Day 21).
2. A pull request sets the dev overlay to `1.2.0`. You merge it, and Argo CD deploys dev.
3. You test dev.
4. A second pull request sets the prod overlay to the same `1.2.0`. Someone reviews and merges it, and Argo CD deploys prod.

The image never gets rebuilt. Prod runs the exact bytes that dev ran, which is the build once, deploy many idea from Day 17. The pull request gives you a review and a record of who approved it. It also gives you a clean undo: the Revert button on a merged pull request opens a new one that puts the old tag back.

This only works if a tag always means the same image. Never deploy `latest`. It points at different images over time, so git no longer tells you what runs, and a revert cannot bring the old version back. That breaks the "versioned and immutable" principle from Day 39. A version tag such as `1.2.0` is good. A digest such as `@sha256:...` is stronger, because nobody can move it, and the `images` field in a kustomization accepts a `digest` too.

Some teams want reviewers to read the full rendered YAML of each environment. Argo CD's Source Hydrator renders each environment and commits the plain YAML to git before it syncs. It is a Beta feature since Argo CD 3.5 and off by default. Tools such as [Kargo](https://github.com/akuity/kargo) and [GitOps Promoter](https://github.com/argoproj-labs/gitops-promoter) go further and automate the promotion steps themselves.

sections.h: Getting a new tag into git
sections.body:
Argo CD deploys only what git says, so something has to write each new tag into a file. Teams use two common ways.

The first is a CI job that edits the file and opens a pull request. The classic tool for the edit is `kustomize edit set image`, run inside an overlay folder. It works, but it rewrites the whole file in its own style. On the lab's prod overlay it changed 80 lines to set one tag, because it drops comments at line ends and re-indents lists. So the lab's `bump-image.yml` workflow uses `yq`, a command line tool for YAML, which changes only the fields you name. You give the workflow an environment and a version, and it:
1. Checks that the version looks like `1.2.0`.
2. Sets `newName` and `newTag` of the `hello-devops` image in that environment's overlay.
3. Pushes a branch and opens a pull request with the `gh` CLI.

New personal repos do not let workflows open pull requests. You allow it once, under Settings, Actions, General, Workflow permissions.

The second way is [Argo CD Image Updater](https://github.com/argoproj-labs/argocd-image-updater), a separate add-on. It watches your registry, and when a version that matches your rule appears, it writes the new tag for you. Since its 1.0 release you configure it with its own custom resource, `ImageUpdater`; the lab's optional `argocd/image-updater.yaml` is one. With the `git` write-back method it commits straight to the branch, with no pull request. Its README says it is under active development and not yet recommended for critical production workloads.

My advice: start with the CI pull request for every environment. If the dev pull requests turn into busywork, let Image Updater handle dev, and keep prod on pull requests.

sections.h: Putting things in order: sync waves and hooks
sections.body:
Argo CD applies everything in one sync, in a sensible default order: Namespaces first, then other built-in kinds, then custom resources. Sometimes you need more control. Redis should be ready before the app starts, or a database migration must finish before new code arrives.

A sync wave is an annotation on any object: `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"`. Argo CD applies the lowest wave first and waits until it is in sync and healthy before it starts the next. Objects without the annotation are in wave 0, and negative numbers are allowed. Argo CD also pauses for 2 seconds between waves.

A hook is an object, usually a Job, that runs at a set point of the sync. You mark it with the annotation `argocd.argoproj.io/hook`:
- `PreSync` runs before anything is applied. If it fails, the sync stops. Use it for a database migration.
- `Sync` runs together with the normal objects.
- `PostSync` runs after everything is applied and Healthy. Use it for a smoke test.
- `SyncFail` runs when the sync fails, for clean-up or an alert.

The lab's `gitops/smoke-test.yaml` is a PostSync hook. It calls `/healthz` once with curl. If curl gets an error, Argo CD marks the sync as failed, and you see it in the UI. A second annotation, `argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy`, decides when Argo CD deletes the finished Job.

One catch: hooks do not run during a selective sync, when you sync only some of an app's objects. Sync the whole app when you want the hooks.

sections.body:
Anyone with access to the repo can read everything in it, and git keeps every old version. A plain Kubernetes Secret is only base64 encoded (Day 34), so committing one is the same as committing the password. Three common ways out:
- Sealed Secrets: you encrypt a Secret on your laptop with `kubeseal` and the cluster's public key, then commit the result, a SealedSecret. Only the controller in that cluster holds the private key that turns it back into a Secret.
- External Secrets Operator: git holds only a pointer, an ExternalSecret that names an entry in a store such as AWS Secrets Manager or Vault. The operator copies the value into a Secret in the cluster.
- SOPS: encrypts the values inside a YAML file with a key from age or a cloud key service. The keys of the file stay readable; the values do not. Flux can decrypt SOPS files itself, while Argo CD needs a plugin.

Argo CD's [secret management](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/secret-management/) page strongly recommends the styles where the Secret is created in the destination cluster, such as the first two. Argo CD never sees the value. It cautions against plugins that inject secrets while Argo CD renders the YAML, because those values then sit in Argo CD's Redis cache in plain text.

hello-devops has no real secrets yet, so the lab needs none of this today. Day 53 goes deeper into secrets, access and policy.

sections.body:
Everything on Day 39 used the `default` project, which allows any repo, any cluster, any namespace and any kind of object. An AppProject narrows that down for a group of apps. The lab's `argocd/project.yaml` allows:
- One source repo: yours.
- Three namespaces in the local cluster: `hello`, `hello-dev` and `hello-prod`.
- No cluster-wide objects except Namespaces.

Point an app in this project at another repo, or at `kube-system`, and Argo CD refuses to sync it. Projects also hold roles: the lab's `viewer` role may look at the apps and read logs, nothing more.

Who may do what in the UI and CLI is Argo CD's own RBAC, separate from Kubernetes RBAC (Day 38). A fresh install has one user, `admin`, who may do everything. Teams connect single sign-on and map groups to roles, either the built-in `role:readonly` and `role:admin` or their own. Argo CD 3.x changed two defaults that older guides get wrong. The right to update or delete an Application no longer covers the objects inside it, and reading Pod logs needs its own `logs` permission.

[Flux](https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2) is the other big GitOps tool. Like Argo CD it is a graduated CNCF project, and the ideas from these two days carry over. The differences are mostly about style:
- Flux is a set of small controllers that you drive with YAML and the `flux` CLI. Its core has no web UI; the separate [Flux Operator](https://fluxoperator.dev/web-ui/) adds one.
- Flux usually runs inside every cluster it manages, while one Argo CD often manages many clusters from one place.
- Flux ships its own image automation controllers and can decrypt SOPS files itself; Argo CD uses Image Updater and plugins.

Choose Argo CD when people want a UI to see and sync apps. Choose Flux when the team wants everything as YAML and no central server.

worked.title: Promote 1.1.0 from dev to prod by hand

steps.say: Ask git, not the cluster, what each environment should run. `kubectl kustomize` renders an overlay on your laptop and never touches the cluster. Dev already runs 1.1.0, and prod still runs 1.0.0. Both are local images in your kind cluster.
steps.code:
$ kubectl kustomize overlays/dev | grep 'image:'
        image: hello-devops:1.1.0
      - image: redis:8-alpine
$ kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | grep 'image:'
        image: hello-devops:1.0.0
      - image: redis:8-alpine

steps.say: Try the classic tool first. The `kustomize edit set image` command sets the tag, but look at the size of the change: it rewrote the whole file, dropping comments at line ends and re-indenting lists. A reviewer would have to hunt for the one line that matters, so throw that edit away.
steps.code:
$ cd overlays/prod
$ kustomize edit set image hello-devops:1.1.0
$ cd ../..
$ git diff --stat
 overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml | 80 ++++++++++++++++++++--------------------
 1 file changed, 40 insertions(+), 40 deletions(-)
$ git checkout -- .

steps.say: `yq` changes only the field you name and keeps everything else, comments included. Now the diff is one line, and the review takes seconds. (`-U1` shows one line of context instead of three.)
steps.code:
$ yq -i '(.images[] | select(.name == "hello-devops")).newTag = "1.1.0"' \
    overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
$ git diff -U1
diff --git a/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml b/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
index dc5f3ef..f0ec01f 100644
--- a/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
+++ b/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
@@ -15,3 +15,3 @@ images:
   - name: hello-devops
-    newTag: "1.0.0" # prod runs the release that already passed dev
+    newTag: "1.1.0" # prod runs the release that already passed dev
 replicas:

steps.say: Check the result before you commit: render prod again and confirm the new tag. This catches a typo in the file before Argo CD ever sees it.
steps.code:
$ kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | grep 'image:'
        image: hello-devops:1.1.0
      - image: redis:8-alpine

steps.say: Ship it like any other change: a branch, a commit and a pull request. Argo CD watches only `main`, so nothing deploys until someone reviews and merges.
steps.code:
$ git switch -c promote/prod-1.1.0
$ git commit -am "Promote hello-devops 1.1.0 to prod"
$ git push -u origin promote/prod-1.1.0
$ gh pr create --fill
$ gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch

steps.say: Within about three minutes Argo CD syncs `hello-devops-prod`, and the rollout replaces the four prod Pods one at a time. Dev was not touched, because its folder did not change. If prod misbehaves, press Revert on the merged pull request and merge the revert: Argo CD puts 1.0.0 back.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello-prod get deployment hello-devops \
    -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'
hello-devops:1.1.0

code.src:
# An Argo CD project: the rules for every hello-devops Application (Day 40).
# It says which repo the apps may read, where they may deploy, and which
# cluster-wide objects they may create. Apply it before applicationset.yaml:
#   kubectl apply -n argocd -f argocd/project.yaml
# Replace <your-github-user> with your GitHub user name first.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: hello
  namespace: argocd
  # Argo CD will not delete this project while an Application still uses it.
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
spec:
  description: hello-devops in dev and prod
  # Apps in this project may only read your repo.
  sourceRepos:
    - https://github.com/<your-github-user>/hello-devops
  # They may only deploy to these namespaces of the cluster Argo CD runs in.
  # (hello is for the Day 39 app, if you move it into this project.)
  destinations:
    - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
      namespace: hello
    - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
      namespace: hello-dev
    - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
      namespace: hello-prod
  # Cluster-wide objects are denied, except Namespaces (the app creates its own).
  clusterResourceWhitelist:
    - group: ""
      kind: Namespace
  # A role you can hand out later, for example to a teammate or a dashboard:
  # it can look at the apps and read their logs, but not sync or delete them.
  roles:
    - name: viewer
      description: Read-only access to hello-devops apps
      policies:
        - p, proj:hello:viewer, applications, get, hello/*, allow
        - p, proj:hello:viewer, logs, get, hello/*, allow

code.title: argocd/applicationset.yaml
code.src:
# An ApplicationSet: one template that makes one Argo CD Application per
# environment (Day 40). Here it makes hello-devops-dev and hello-devops-prod.
# Each one deploys a Kustomize overlay from your repo into its own namespace.
# Apply it after project.yaml:
#   kubectl apply -n argocd -f argocd/applicationset.yaml
# Replace <your-github-user> with your GitHub user name first.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  # Use Go templates ({{.env}}) and stop with an error on a misspelled name.
  goTemplate: true
  goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
  # The generator makes one set of values per environment.
  generators:
    - list:
        elements:
          - env: dev
            namespace: hello-dev
          - env: prod
            namespace: hello-prod
  # The template is a normal Application with {{.env}} and {{.namespace}} filled in.
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "hello-devops-{{.env}}"
      labels:
        env: "{{.env}}"
    spec:
      project: hello # the rules in project.yaml
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/<your-github-user>/hello-devops
        targetRevision: main
        path: "overlays/{{.env}}" # the Kustomize overlay for this environment (Day 37)
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: "{{.namespace}}"
      # Same reason as in application.yaml: the autoscaler owns the replica count.
      ignoreDifferences:
        - group: apps
          kind: Deployment
          name: hello-devops
          jsonPointers:
            - /spec/replicas
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true # delete things that you removed from git
          selfHeal: true # undo changes made by hand in the cluster
        syncOptions:
          - CreateNamespace=true
          - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true

code.src:
# Opens a pull request that changes which image version one environment runs (Day 40).
# Save it as .github/workflows/bump-image.yml in your repo. (This reference copy
# sits in gitops/ so that it never runs in the course's own repo.)
# Once, before the first run: Settings > Actions > General > Workflow permissions,
# tick "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests".
# Run it from the Actions tab, or with:
#   gh workflow run bump-image.yml -f environment=dev -f version=1.2.0
name: bump-image

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        description: Which environment to change
        type: choice
        options: [dev, prod]
        default: dev
      version:
        description: Image tag to deploy, such as 1.2.0 (no "v" in front)
        type: string
        required: true

# Only what this job needs: push a branch and open a pull request.
permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write

# One bump per environment at a time.
concurrency:
  group: bump-image-${{ inputs.environment }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  bump:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    env:
      # Inputs go through env variables, never straight into a script.
      ENVIRONMENT: ${{ inputs.environment }}
      VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
      FILE: overlays/${{ inputs.environment }}/kustomization.yaml
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Check the inputs
        run: |
          if [[ ! "$VERSION" =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]]; then
            echo "::error::Version must look like 1.2.0, got '$VERSION'"
            exit 1
          fi
          if [ -z "$(yq '.images[] | select(.name == "hello-devops") | .name' "$FILE")" ]; then
            echo "::error::$FILE has no images entry named hello-devops"
            exit 1
          fi

      # yq (already installed on GitHub's ubuntu runners) changes only these two
      # fields and keeps every comment. `kustomize edit set image` does the same
      # job, but it rewrites the whole file and drops comments at line ends.
      - name: Write the new image into the overlay
        run: |
          # The same lower case image name that release.yml pushes to.
          export IMAGE="ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}"
          yq -i '(.images[] | select(.name == "hello-devops")) |=
            (.newName = strenv(IMAGE) | .newTag = strenv(VERSION))' "$FILE"
          git diff

      - name: Open a pull request
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          if git diff --quiet; then
            echo "The $ENVIRONMENT overlay already uses $VERSION. Nothing to do."
            exit 0
          fi
          BRANCH="bump/${ENVIRONMENT}-${VERSION}"
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git switch -c "$BRANCH"
          git commit -am "Deploy hello-devops ${VERSION} to ${ENVIRONMENT}"
          git push origin "$BRANCH"
          gh pr create --base main --head "$BRANCH" \
            --title "Deploy hello-devops ${VERSION} to ${ENVIRONMENT}" \
            --body "Sets the hello-devops image in ${FILE}. Argo CD deploys it after you merge."
          {
            echo "### Pull request opened"
            echo "Branch \`$BRANCH\` sets $ENVIRONMENT to $VERSION."
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

code.src:
# A PostSync hook (Day 40): after every sync, once all resources are Healthy,
# Argo CD runs this Job. If curl fails, Argo CD marks the sync as failed.
# To try it, copy this file into overlays/dev/ and add
# "- smoke-test.yaml" to the resources list in that kustomization.yaml.
# The overlay moves it into namespace hello-dev, next to the hello-devops Service.
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: smoke-test
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PostSync
    # Delete the old Job just before the next sync creates a new one.
    # Until then you can still read its logs.
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0 # one try only: a failure fails the sync
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: curl
          image: curlimages/curl:8.22.0
          # -f: fail on an HTTP error, -sS: quiet but show errors, -m 5: give up after 5 seconds.
          # hello-devops is the Service name in this namespace, on port 80.
          args: ["-fsS", "-m", "5", "http://hello-devops/healthz"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 10m
              memory: 16Mi
            limits:
              memory: 32Mi

code.src:
# OPTIONAL (Day 40): let Argo CD Image Updater move dev to each new release.
# You only need this file if you install Argo CD Image Updater (see its docs).
# It watches your image in GHCR and, when a higher 1.x version appears,
# commits the new image into overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml on main.
# It commits straight to main, with no pull request, so keep it to dev.
# Before you apply it:
#   1. Replace <your-github-user> below.
#   2. Create a Secret named git-creds in namespace argocd with two keys:
#      username (your GitHub user) and password (a fine-grained token that can
#      write to the hello-devops repo only).
# Apply it with: kubectl apply -n argocd -f argocd/image-updater.yaml
apiVersion: argocd-image-updater.argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ImageUpdater
metadata:
  name: hello-devops-dev
  namespace: argocd # the namespace of the Applications it updates
spec:
  # Write the new tag to git, using the token in the git-creds Secret.
  # (The default method, argocd, changes only the Application in the cluster.)
  writeBackConfig:
    method: git:secret:git-creds
    gitConfig:
      branch: main
      # Edit the overlay's kustomization.yaml, as `kustomize edit set image` would.
      writeBackTarget: kustomization
  applicationRefs:
    - namePattern: hello-devops-dev # only the dev Application
      images:
        - alias: app
          # ":1.x" is a version rule: any 1.something version, never 2.0.0.
          imageName: ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/hello-devops:1.x
          commonUpdateSettings:
            updateStrategy: semver # pick the highest version that fits the rule
            # Dev may still run the image that kind loaded (hello-devops:1.1.0),
            # which has a different name, so update even if no GHCR image runs yet.
            forceUpdate: true
          manifestTargets:
            kustomize:
              name: hello-devops # the image name in k8s/deployment.yaml

lessons.mistake: Deploying `latest` and expecting GitOps to handle versions. If an overlay says `latest`, git does not change when the image does, so Argo CD sees nothing to sync and a revert brings nothing back. Give every release its own version tag (or pin a digest), and promote by changing that tag in git.
lessons.real_world: A payments team might run dev, staging and prod clusters from one config repo, with one ApplicationSet per app that uses the cluster generator. CI opens the dev pull request after every release and merges it once checks pass. Prod needs a second pull request, approved by someone on the on-call rotation, and a PostSync smoke test fails the sync if checkout stops answering.

task.title: Run dev and prod from one ApplicationSet
steps: Add `argocd/project.yaml` and `argocd/applicationset.yaml` with your GitHub user name. Commit, push, and apply both. The Day 39 app can stay, because the overlays use ClusterIP Services.

Check that `hello-devops-dev` and `hello-devops-prod` appear and both turn Synced and Healthy. Dev uses the local image `hello-devops:1.1.0`; if kind lacks it, run `kind load docker-image hello-devops:1.1.0 --name devops`.
Port-forward to the dev and the prod Service in turn, and check with curl that each one greets you differently.
Add `.github/workflows/bump-image.yml`, push it, and allow workflows to create pull requests in the repo settings.
Push a new release tag, for example `v1.2.0`, and wait for `release.yml` to finish. Make the GHCR package public, so kind can pull it without a password.
Run the bump workflow for dev with version `1.2.0`. Read the pull request: it should change two lines in `overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml`. Merge it.
Confirm that dev now runs `ghcr.io/<you>/hello-devops:1.2.0` while prod still runs its old tag.
Promote: run the workflow again for prod with the same version, merge, and confirm that both environments match.
Optional: add the smoke-test hook to the dev overlay, then break its URL and watch the dev sync fail.
hints: Checks may not start on their own for a pull request that the workflow opened with `GITHUB_TOKEN`; GitHub does this to stop workflow loops. If the merge box asks you to approve the workflow runs, approve them.
ImagePullBackOff after a bump usually means the GHCR package is still private, or the tag does not exist. `kubectl -n hello-dev describe pod` names the exact image it tried.
Unsure what a bump will change? Save the output of `kubectl kustomize overlays/dev` to a file before and after, then compare the two with `diff`.
task.done_when: You are done when the jsonpath command from the Commands list prints the same `ghcr.io/.../hello-devops:1.2.0` image for `hello-dev` and `hello-prod`, and both apps are Synced and Healthy.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate, in 3 to 4 sentences, how version 1.3.0 travels from a git tag to prod in this setup. Mention who builds the image, what changes in git, and what Argo CD does.
explain_back.answer: Pushing the tag v1.3.0 starts release.yml, which builds the image once and pushes it to GHCR as 1.3.0. A workflow then opens a pull request that sets the dev overlay to 1.3.0; after the merge, Argo CD sees the commit and deploys dev. When dev looks good, a second pull request copies the same tag into the prod overlay, someone reviews it, and Argo CD deploys prod. If prod breaks, reverting that pull request puts the old tag back.

recap: Deployment YAML lives in git, in the app repo or a separate config repo with cleaner history and access.
Each environment gets one overlay and one Application; an ApplicationSet writes the Applications from one template.
Promotion is a pull request that copies a tested, immutable tag to the next overlay. Never deploy latest.
CI writes the new tag with a small edit (yq or kustomize edit set image) and opens a pull request; Image Updater can do it for dev.
Sync waves order objects, hooks run Jobs before or after a sync, and secrets stay out of git as Sealed or External Secrets.
AppProjects limit repos, namespaces and kinds. Flux is the main alternative to Argo CD.

An ApplicationSet can make at most two Applications
Staging needs its own Argo CD install to work

check.why: The AppProject lists the allowed destinations, so you also have to add hello-staging to project.yaml.

check.q: Image Updater runs with the lab's settings and finds a new version 1.4.0. What appears in your repo?
options: A pull request that waits for your review
Nothing; it patches only the live Deployment
A new git tag v1.4.0 on the main branch
A commit on main that changes the dev kustomization
check.why: With git write-back and the kustomization target, it commits straight to the tracked branch, with no pull request.

check.q: A Job marked `argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync` runs a database migration and fails. What happens to the new app version?
options: Argo CD applies it anyway and marks the sync failed
The sync stops before the other objects are applied
Argo CD retries the Job until the migration passes
The Job is skipped and the sync carries on as usual
check.why: A failed PreSync hook stops the whole sync, so new code never meets an old database schema.

interview.q: How do you promote a release between environments with GitOps?
interview.a: CI builds the image once and tags it with a version, never latest. Each environment has its own folder, for example a Kustomize overlay, and promotion is a pull request that copies the tested tag or digest from one folder to the next. The review is the approval, and the merge is the deploy, because Argo CD or Flux syncs the change. Rolling back is a revert of that pull request.

interview.q: How do you handle secrets when everything lives in git?
interview.a: I never commit plain Secrets, because base64 is not encryption and git keeps history forever. One option is to commit encrypted SealedSecrets that only the in-cluster controller can decrypt. The other is to commit ExternalSecret references and let the External Secrets Operator fetch the values from a store such as Vault or AWS Secrets Manager. Argo CD recommends these destination-cluster styles. I avoid plugins that inject secrets while Argo CD renders manifests, because those values land in its cache.

interview.q: When would you choose Flux over Argo CD?
interview.a: Both are graduated CNCF projects that pull from git and reconcile, so the core idea is the same. I would pick Argo CD when people want a web UI to see app health and sync by hand, or when one central instance should manage many clusters. I would pick Flux when the team prefers everything as YAML and the CLI, runs one controller set per cluster, and wants image automation and SOPS decryption built in. Either way, the repo layout and promotion flow look much the same.

deeper.body:
Your setup is one cluster with two namespaces. A company with fifty clusters uses the same ideas, only generated.

Start with the generator. The cluster generator makes one Application per cluster that Argo CD knows. It can filter by labels on those clusters, such as `env: prod` or `region: eu`. Register a new cluster with the right labels, and every matching ApplicationSet deploys to it. The [Argo CD docs on cluster bootstrapping](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/cluster-bootstrapping/) recommend exactly this for new clusters. The matrix generator combines two generators, for example every folder under `apps/` times every cluster labelled `env: dev`.

Then decide where Argo CD itself runs:
- Hub and spoke: one Argo CD in a management cluster deploys to all the others. You get one UI and one place for access rules. If the hub is down, nothing new deploys, though running apps keep running.
- One Argo CD per cluster: no single point of failure, but more installs to upgrade. This is also the usual Flux model.

Changing fifty clusters at once is risky. ApplicationSet Progressive Syncs, a Beta feature, update the generated apps in steps. For example, dev clusters go first, then a few prod clusters, then the rest, and each step waits until the previous one is healthy.

Last, the rendered manifests pattern. With overlays and charts, a one-line change in a base can change the YAML of every environment, and the pull request does not show it. The Source Hydrator (Beta since Argo CD 3.5, off by default) renders each environment, commits the plain YAML to a separate branch, and syncs from there. Reviewers then read the exact YAML that will run, and `git diff` between two commits shows exactly what changed in prod.

You can get a cheap version of this today. In a pull request check, run `kubectl kustomize` for each overlay on both the main branch and the pull request branch, and post the diff as a comment. A reviewer who sees "prod: replicas 3 to 6" catches mistakes that "k8s/deployment.yaml: one line changed" hides.

sources.title: Argo CD: sync phases and waves

recap: GitOps: git holds the desired state, and an agent in the cluster pulls it and reconciles.
Pull deploys keep cluster credentials out of CI and turn every deploy into a commit.
Argo CD 3.x installs with server-side apply and tracks its objects with an annotation.
Sync status (does it match git?) and health (does it work?) are separate signals.
Self-heal and prune are off by default; ignore fields that other controllers own.
Roll back with git revert or the Revert button on the pull request.
One overlay and one Application per environment; an ApplicationSet generates the Applications.
Promotion copies a tested, immutable tag to the next environment through a pull request.
Secrets stay out of git through Sealed Secrets, External Secrets or SOPS; AppProjects and RBAC limit who deploys where.

flashcards.front: What are the four OpenGitOps principles?
flashcards.back: Declarative; versioned and immutable; pulled automatically; continuously reconciled.

flashcards.front: Push deploy or pull deploy: which one needs a cluster key in CI?
flashcards.back: Push. In a pull deploy, an agent inside the cluster fetches from git and applies.

flashcards.front: Why does installing Argo CD 3.x need kubectl apply --server-side?
flashcards.back: The ApplicationSet definition is too big for the annotation that client-side apply writes.
Sync: does the cluster match git? Health: do the objects work?

flashcards.front: What does selfHeal do, and is it on by default?
flashcards.back: It undoes changes made in the cluster but not in git. It is off by default.

flashcards.front: What does prune do, and is it on by default?
flashcards.back: It deletes objects you removed from git. It is off by default.

flashcards.front: How does Argo CD 3.x remember which app owns an object?
flashcards.back: The annotation argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id on that object.

flashcards.front: How often does Argo CD check git by default?
flashcards.back: About every 3 minutes (120 s plus up to 60 s of jitter). A webhook makes it immediate.
So Argo CD and the autoscaler do not fight over the replica count.

flashcards.front: How do you roll back an app that Argo CD syncs automatically?
flashcards.back: Revert the commit or pull request in git. Argo CD deploys the old state.
A template plus generators that create many Applications, for example one per environment.
A pull request that copies a tested image tag from one environment's folder to the next.

flashcards.front: Why never deploy the latest tag with GitOps?
flashcards.back: Git does not change when the image does, so you cannot see or revert what runs.

flashcards.front: What does kustomize edit set image do, and what is the catch?
flashcards.back: It sets an image name and tag in the kustomization.yaml of the current folder, but rewrites the whole file and drops comments at line ends.

flashcards.front: When does a PostSync hook run?
flashcards.back: After all objects are applied and Healthy. A smoke test is a typical use.

flashcards.front: Which secret styles does Argo CD recommend?
flashcards.back: Ones that create the Secret in the cluster, such as Sealed Secrets or External Secrets Operator.
Which repos, clusters, namespaces and kinds of objects its apps may use.

flashcards.front: Main style difference between Flux and Argo CD?
flashcards.back: Flux: controllers in each cluster, driven by YAML and CLI. Argo CD: often one central server with a web UI.

quiz.q: Automated sync is on and selfHeal is off. A teammate edits the live ConfigMap by hand. What do you see in Argo CD?
options: The edit is undone within a few seconds
The app shows OutOfSync, and the edit stays for now
The app shows Degraded until someone syncs it
Argo CD commits the edit into git for you
quiz.why: Without self-heal, live changes do not trigger a sync. The drift is reported and stays until the next commit is synced.

quiz.q: Which Argo CD component turns your Kustomize folder into plain YAML?
options: The application controller
The API server
The repository server
The Dex server
quiz.why: The repo server clones the repo and renders Kustomize or Helm; the controller then compares and applies.

quiz.q: You follow an old video and run plain `kubectl apply -n argocd -f install.yaml`. It fails on the ApplicationSet definition. What is the fix?
options: Add --server-side --force-conflicts to the apply
Install an older Kubernetes version in kind
Delete the ApplicationSet definition from the file
Run the same command again until it passes
quiz.why: That definition is too large for client-side apply's annotation; server-side apply does not write that annotation.

quiz.q: After a tag change in git, your app stays Synced and Progressing for many minutes. What is the most likely cause?
options: Argo CD cannot reach the git repository
Self-heal is fighting with the autoscaler
The project forbids the destination namespace
The new Pods cannot start, for example the image cannot be pulled
quiz.why: Synced means the cluster has what git says; a rollout that never finishes points at the new Pods themselves.

quiz.q: Why does promotion copy the same image tag to prod instead of building a fresh image for prod?
options: GHCR allows only one push per version
Prod then runs exactly the bytes that were tested in dev
Building twice would cost extra GitHub Actions minutes only
Argo CD cannot deploy images built from a branch
quiz.why: Build once, deploy many: a rebuild could pick up new dependencies and ship something nobody tested.

quiz.q: Argo CD synced a new GREETING into hello-config, but curl still returns the old greeting. Why?
options: Argo CD has not pruned the old ConfigMap yet
The ConfigMap needs a sync wave of -1
The Pods read env variables only at start, so they need a restart
The Service still points at the old ReplicaSet
quiz.why: Environment variables from a ConfigMap are read when the container starts; restart the Deployment, or generate a new ConfigMap name.

quiz.q: How should a database password for hello-devops reach the cluster in a GitOps setup?
options: Commit an encrypted SealedSecret that only the cluster can decrypt
Commit a normal Secret, since base64 hides the value
Put it in the ConfigMap, then use a private repo
Type it with kubectl create secret and leave it out of git
quiz.why: A SealedSecret is safe in git and is decrypted only in the cluster; a hand-made Secret works but drifts outside git.

quiz.q: You want a staging environment between dev and prod in this lab. What is the least you must add?
options: A second Argo CD install in a staging namespace
A copy of application.yaml for every Kubernetes object
A new branch called staging with its own k8s folder
An overlay folder, a generator entry, and the namespace in the project
quiz.why: The ApplicationSet makes the app from the new entry, the overlay holds its settings, and the project must allow the namespace.

quiz.q: Which statement about Flux and Argo CD is accurate?
options: Only Argo CD can deploy Kustomize overlays
Both pull from git and reconcile; Flux has image automation built in
Flux pushes changes from CI into the cluster
Argo CD is a CNCF project, while Flux is not
quiz.why: Both are graduated CNCF GitOps tools. Flux ships image automation controllers; Argo CD uses the separate Image Updater.
